articles.title: Nicotine-free vaping may still harm blood vessels – small MRI study
articles.author: David C. Gaze, Senior Lecturer in Chemical Pathology, University of Westminster
paras: A nicotine-free vape sounds like a safer choice. Yet new research found that just one session of vaping, with no nicotine in it, can affect how blood vessels work.

The study, which was presented at the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America, identified changes in blood flow and oxygen levels following just one episode of vaping, regardless of whether the e-cigarette contained nicotine. The findings raise an important question. Have we been focusing too much on nicotine and not enough on what else we are inhaling?

E-cigarettes, commonly known as vapes, are battery-powered devices that heat a liquid to produce an aerosol vapour. Unlike conventional cigarettes, they do not burn tobacco, meaning users are exposed to fewer harmful chemicals.

The cloud that people inhale and exhale, however, is not simply water vapour. Most vaping liquids contain a mixture of propylene glycol, vegetable glycerine and flavouring chemicals. Although some of these ingredients are used in food production, eating a substance is not the same as inhaling it.

When heated, these liquids can produce potentially harmful chemicals, including formaldehyde and acrolein. Research has also identified tiny particles of metals, including nickel, chromium and lead, in vaping aerosols. Some originate from the metal coil used to heat the liquid. Simply removing the nicotine does not remove these substances.
What happens in blood vessels?
Blood vessels are more than a network of pipes transporting blood around the body. They are living structures that constantly adjust to the changing demands of our organs.

The inner lining of our blood vessels, known as the endothelium, produces a chemical called nitric oxide. This allows blood vessels to relax and widen, increasing blood flow when our tissues need more oxygen.

When we exercise, for example, blood vessels widen to deliver more oxygen to our working muscles. When this process becomes impaired, it is known as endothelial dysfunction, which is a very early feature of cardiovascular disease.

In the latest study, researchers recruited 41 otherwise healthy adults, aged between 20 and 50, who had smoked, vaped or used both products daily for more than a year. A further 17 people who had never smoked or vaped acted as a comparison (control) group.

Using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), researchers examined participants before and after three separate activities: smoking a cigarette, vaping with nicotine and vaping without nicotine. They measured several aspects of cardiovascular health, including how effectively blood vessels responded to changing oxygen demands and the stiffness of the aorta, the largest artery in the body.

Following all three activities, researchers found a reduction in the amount of oxygen remaining in blood returning from the leg. This could suggest that vaping temporarily interferes with the ability to transfer oxygen in the lungs into the bloodstream, although changes in blood flow and oxygen use by tissues could also explain the findings.

Surprisingly, vaping affected more of the measurements investigated than smoking did. This does not mean that vaping is more harmful than smoking. But it does challenge the assumption that nicotine-free vaping is harmless.

These findings chime with earlier research. In a study published in 2019, 31 healthy non-smokers were exposed to nicotine-free vaping aerosol. After a single session, the ability of an artery in the leg to widen in response to increased blood flow was reduced by 34%.
A 2022 study also found that regular e-cigarette users and cigarette smokers had poorer blood vessel function than non-users.

More recently, research published in 2025 found that smoking and vaping can affect how well the blood vessels supplying the heart regulate blood flow. This means the vessels may be less able to increase the blood supply to the heart when it needs more oxygen, such as during exercise.

One possible explanation is oxidative stress, which occurs when the body produces more reactive molecules than it can get rid of. These molecules can reduce levels of nitric oxide and cause inflammation, which can damage blood vessels and contribute to heart disease.

However, not all studies agree. A clinical trial published in 2018 found changes in blood vessel function following vaping with nicotine, but not without it. Differences in vaping devices, ingredients and research methods may partly explain these conflicting findings.

The latest study involved relatively few people and looked only at short-term effects. It is still unclear whether repeated exposure causes lasting harm or increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes.
It is important not to overlook the benefits of vaping for people trying to stop smoking.
A large, well-conducted review found that nicotine-containing e-cigarettes were more effective at helping people quit smoking than nicotine replacement products such as patches and gum.
The NHS advises that vaping is less harmful than smoking but is not risk-free.

Nicotine-free vaping may remove the addictive ingredient, but it does not remove all the potential health risks. Being nicotine-free is not the same as being harm-free. And that is a distinction that should not be overlooked.

articles.title: GTA 6: four surprising ways playing video games could benefit your health
articles.author: George Farmer, PhD Candidate, Video Gaming and Psychological Wellbeing, Westminster University
paras: After 13 years of anticipation, Grand Theft Auto 6 has finally arrived, with fans around the world celebrating the latest instalment of one of gaming’s most successful franchises.
The excitement surrounding its release has also brought renewed attention to a familiar debate: what effect does playing video games have on us?

Gaming has long been associated with concerns about addiction and social isolation. But depending on what we play and how we engage with it, gaming can offer benefits for our cognitive abilities, social lives and physical and mental wellbeing.
1. Developing cognitive skills

Playing an action game such as Grand Theft Auto can be mentally demanding. Navigating a busy virtual city while driving, monitoring your surroundings and responding to unexpected events requires considerable attention and an ability to process information quickly.
A 2022 study of 163 adults compared regular action video game players, whose preferred games included Grand Theft Auto and Assassin’s Creed, with people who rarely or never played video games.

The gamers performed better on tests of mental rotation, the ability to imagine how an object would look if turned in a different direction. They were also more accurate at keeping track of multiple moving objects.
However, the researchers could not establish whether gaming had developed these abilities or whether people with stronger spatial and attentional skills were naturally drawn to action games.

A review of experimental studies found that playing action games could improve our ability to focus on relevant information while ignoring distractions, as well as our understanding of spatial relationships. These skills are useful in everyday activities such as navigating unfamiliar places.
However, researchers continue to debate how far the skills developed through gaming translate into broader improvements in our thinking and learning.
2. Building social connections

Despite the perception that gaming is an isolating activity, many modern games are designed around interaction with other people. Online multiplayer games allow players to communicate, collaborate and maintain friendships across geographical distances.

A study of 2,213 gamers and 287 non-gamers in Germany found that social gamers were generally as well connected as non-gamers, and that spending more time playing socially increased the likelihood of forming friendships online. These connections became particularly valuable during the COVID pandemic, when people had fewer opportunities to meet in person.

Some games also encourage players to work together towards a shared goal. In massively multiplayer online games, where large numbers of people play in the same virtual world, team members may need to plan their approach and share information.

For instance, research into team communication in the game World of Tanks found that higher-ranked teams tended to communicate more before battles, although this does not establish that gaming improves teamwork outside the game.
Of course, online gaming communities can expose players to harassment or abusive behaviour. The social experience depends on the game, its community and the people involved.
3. Promoting wellbeing and relieving stress
Gaming can be something to look forward to after a long day at work, offering a chance to relax and put everyday responsibilities aside.

Completing a difficult level or overcoming an obstacle can also satisfy our psychological need for competence: the feeling that we are capable of achieving something. Even an unsuccessful attempt gives players an opportunity to adjust their approach and try again.

Games often described as “cosy” are particularly appealing to people who prefer a slower pace, achievable goals and a relaxed atmosphere. My personal favourite is the Animal Crossing series, in which players live alongside animal characters and take on tasks such as gardening and crafting.

In interviews with 27 families, researchers found that Animal Crossing: New Horizons helped some parents and children cope with pandemic-related stress. The National Videogame Museum’s Animal Crossing Diaries collects players’ experiences of the game during the pandemic.

Some games are designed specifically for health or education rather than entertainment alone. Known as “serious games”, they can be used as part of mental health interventions. A review of therapeutic games for young people found promising effects on anxiety and depression, although more rigorous research is needed.
4. Encouraging physical activity
Not all gaming involves sitting still. “Exergames” incorporate physical movement into play, through activities such as dancing or sports simulations.

These games can make exercise more appealing to people who find conventional workouts less engaging. Research on virtual-reality exercise suggests that adding game elements can increase enjoyment during high-intensity interval training.

My favourite example of a game that encourages physical activity is Pokémon Go. It encourages players to walk around their neighbourhoods to collect digital creatures and visit locations, using augmented reality to add virtual objects to a view of the real world.

A study using fitness trackers found that the most engaged Pokémon Go players increased their activity by an average of nearly 1,500 steps a day over a month. Whether that increase lasts in the longer term is less clear.
None of these benefits is guaranteed. Gaming can become harmful when it interferes with sleep, work, education or relationships.

The World Health Organization recognises gaming disorder as a condition involving impaired control over gaming and continued play despite significant negative consequences. Simply spending a lot of time playing does not amount to a diagnosis.
Why people play also matters. A review of research linked playing primarily to escape distressing experiences with problematic gaming, although those studies could not establish cause and effect.
Meanwhile, a large Oxford study found little evidence that the amount of time spent playing, on its own, substantially affected wellbeing.
While it is too early to establish the specific cognitive benefits of playing Grand Theft Auto 6, research into similar games suggests that navigating its virtual world could have some benefits.
Rather than judging all video games as good or bad, it is more useful to consider what people get from the games they enjoy and how gaming fits into the rest of their lives.

articles.title: Alzheimer’s drug targets tau protein in promising clinical trial
articles.author: Rahul Sidhu, PhD Candidate, Neuroscience, University of Sheffield
paras: An experimental Alzheimer’s drug that reduces the production of a protein called tau has slowed the decline in memory and thinking skills by up to 54% in a clinical trial.

The drug, called diranersen, works differently from approved Alzheimer’s treatments. These focus on clearing amyloid, one of two proteins that build up abnormally in the brain. Diranersen targets the other protein – tau.

Amyloid forms sticky plaques between brain cells, while tau clumps together inside them, forming tangled structures. Both proteins damage brain cells, disrupting the signals they use to communicate and the processes that keep them alive.
Tau has an important job in a healthy brain. It helps stabilise tiny structures called microtubules, which act like railway tracks, transporting nutrients and other materials around brain cells.

In Alzheimer’s, tau changes structure, detaches from these tracks and clumps together inside brain cells, forming tangles. These tangles interfere with the cell’s internal transport system, contributing to its eventual death. The amount of tau accumulating in the brain is closely linked to how quickly people’s thinking skills decline.

Two drugs, lecanemab and donanemab, have been approved by most regulators (including in the US, Europe and the UK) for treating people with early-stage Alzheimer’s, although they are not available on the NHS.

Both help to remove amyloid plaques from the brain and modestly slow the decline in memory and thinking skills. Neither targets tau, and both can cause significant side-effects, including brain bleeds.

Researchers have found it harder to develop drugs that target tau. Several experimental treatments have used antibodies designed to recognise and destroy abnormal tau. However, these drugs have struggled to improve patients’ symptoms. The problem is that tau builds up inside brain cells, where antibodies find it difficult to reach.
Diranersen takes a different approach. Instead of trying to remove tangles that have already formed, it reduces how much tau brain cells produce in the first place.

The drug was tested in a phase 2 clinical trial, involving 416 people with early Alzheimer’s disease. Phase 2 is the stage when researchers investigate whether a drug appears to work and which dose is most effective.

The most promising results – which are yet to be peer-reviewed – came from the group given the lowest dose (60mg twice a year as an injection in the spine). After 96 weeks, 60 people taking this lower dose had 38% less decline compared with 115 participants originally assigned to placebo on a scale measuring memory, thinking skills and ability to carry out everyday activities.
On a separate test of cognitive performance, their decline was 54% slower. A third measure, assessing everyday activities, showed 30% less decline.

Most side-effects were mild. The most common were pain and headaches linked to the spinal injections, and short spells of confusion that typically cleared up within a week. The researchers found no new safety problems over the two years of follow-up.
Diranersen is a gene-silencing drug. It belongs to a class of medicines called antisense oligonucleotides, which are designed to switch off specific genetic instructions.
The drug attaches to messenger RNA – the molecule that carries the instructions for making tau – and causes it to break down. Without these instructions, brain cells make less of the protein.

Reducing tau raises an important question: could lowering a protein that brain cells need to function also cause harm? Studies in mice have suggested that substantially reducing tau does not significantly disrupt these processes, and the trial found no serious short-term side-effects. But nobody knows whether lowering tau in people is safe over many years.
How strong is the evidence?

There are important reasons to be cautious about the two-year results. They come from an extension of the original trial in which participants and researchers knew who was receiving the drug. After a year and a half, participants who had initially received a placebo were switched to diranersen. This meant researchers could no longer compare the drug with a placebo group over the full two years.

The original 18-month trial also failed to meet its main objective, which was to show that different doses produced a clear difference in clinical decline. Although some other measures showed improvements, missing this main target makes it harder to know how much confidence to place in the longer-term findings.
What is needed next is a much larger phase 3 trial, comparing the drug with a placebo in many more people. Regulators would want to see the results of such a trial before considering it for approval.

For years, Alzheimer’s research has concentrated on amyloid. Targeting tau offers another possible way to tackle the disease. Combining drugs that act on both proteins might eventually prove more effective than either approach alone. But both possibilities still need to be tested in larger trials.

articles.title: Creatine is popular with bodybuilders – could it help older adults stay independent?
articles.author: Alexandra Cremona, Lecturer, Human Nutrition and Dietetics, University of Limerick
paras: Climbing stairs or getting out of a chair can become harder with age, partly because muscle mass and strength tend to decline.

Resistance training, such as lifting weights or exercising with resistance bands, can help maintain muscle strength in later life. Research suggests that creatine, a supplement more commonly associated with bodybuilders and athletes, may help older adults gain a little more strength from this type of exercise. Whether that makes everyday tasks easier or helps people stay independent for longer is less clear.

Creatine is a naturally occurring compound that the body makes from amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. It’s also found in foods such as meat and fish. Most of the body’s creatine is stored in muscle, where it helps replenish the energy needed for short bursts of intense activity, such as lifting weights.

Taking creatine increases the amount available in muscles. That may let people complete a few more repetitions before their muscles tire. Over time, that extra work could help explain some of the gains in strength.
Muscle strength in later life

A 2026 review of 11 randomised trials found that adults aged 60 and over who added creatine to a resistance training programme gained slightly more strength than those who did the training without creatine. The review found no clear improvement in muscle mass or in how well people performed physical tasks.

Participants were generally healthy and were 67 on average, so the findings tell us less about people in their 80s and beyond. It’s also unclear whether the same benefits apply to people with sarcopenia, a condition in which low muscle strength is accompanied by reduced muscle mass or quality.

An earlier review found that people who took creatine gained about 1.3kg more lean tissue, on average, than those who took a placebo while following the same training programme. Measures of lean tissue include water. Creatine can make muscles hold more water, especially in the first few days, so it’s difficult to tell how much of that increase was new muscle.
When people take creatine without doing resistance training, some small studies suggest their muscles take longer to tire. The evidence for gains in strength is clearer for people who also train.
Everyday movement and falls

One way researchers test whether strength gains carry over into daily life is with the sit-to-stand test, also known as the chair-rise test. Researchers count how many times someone can stand up in 30 seconds or time how long it takes them to stand up five times, usually without using their arms for support.

A 2026 review pooled results from five trials of the chair-rise test. Middle-aged and older adults who added creatine to their training performed better than those who trained and took a placebo. The evidence for walking and balance was limited and inconsistent.

In a two-year trial involving 237 postmenopausal women, whose average age was 59, both groups were asked to do resistance training and walk regularly. On average, the women taking creatine walked 80 metres about 1.5 seconds faster than they had at the start of the trial, while the placebo group’s time barely changed. There was no clear difference in reported falls through the end of the third year. The trial was designed to study bone health, so it gives limited information about whether creatine affects the risk of falling.

Research involving frailer older adults is also limited. In two trials involving people who were frail or at risk of frailty, participants got stronger with resistance training. Adding creatine produced no clear extra benefit. There is still too little evidence to say whether creatine helps older people avoid falls or remain independent for longer.
The brain also uses creatine to help maintain its energy supply. This has led researchers to investigate whether taking creatine might help preserve memory in later life.

A review focused on older adults found just two studies that tested supplements. They reached different conclusions. The other studies estimated how much creatine people got from food, so they could only identify links between intake and performance on cognitive tests. There is too little evidence to say whether taking creatine can slow cognitive decline or prevent dementia.
What to know about taking creatine

Creatine monohydrate is the most widely studied form. Some trials have used 3 to 5g a day, while others have used higher doses. The amount that might improve everyday physical function is still uncertain.

Creatine is generally well tolerated at the doses studied. Some people report stomach discomfort, and the extra water in muscle can lead to weight gain. Studies in people with healthy kidneys have generally found no evidence of reduced kidney function. There is less evidence on safety for people with kidney disease.

Creatine can raise blood levels of creatinine, a natural waste product, which is produced when the body breaks down creatine. Because blood tests use creatinine to estimate how well the kidneys are working, taking the supplement can make those results harder to interpret. Research on interactions with prescription medicines is limited. If you have kidney disease or take several prescription medicines, check with a GP or pharmacist before starting.

For older adults who want to stay strong, regular strength exercises are the place to start. NHS guidance for adults aged 65 and over recommends exercise to build strength and improve balance and flexibility on at least two days a week. For people who already do resistance training, creatine may offer a small extra gain in muscle strength.
Alexandra Cremona receives funding from the University of Limerick, Ireland.

articles.title: Mpox cases are on the rise again in Brazil – just as an antiviral drug fails in trials
articles.author: Klinger Soares Faico Filho, Professor de Clínica Médica e Medicina Laboratorial, Universidade Federal de São Paulo (UNIFESP)
paras: The city of Rio de Janeiro has reported 180 confirmed cases of mpox, an infectious disease caused by the monkeypox virus, MPXV, from Oct. 1 through Nov. 24, 2026.

Skin lesions are the most common sign of the disease. They can also appear in the mouth, on the genitals or in the anal region. Other symptoms include fever, swollen glands, headache, body aches, chills and weakness.

The number of cases in the capital of Rio de Janeiro is more than 22 times higher than the number reported during the same period in 2025. In the state of São Paulo, 128 cases have been identified from Oct.1 through Nov. 17, which represents almost half of all cases of the disease that the state has reported this year.
The national figures are not alarming: 1,429 confirmed cases and one death as of Nov. 23, compared to about 10,500 cases and 14 deaths in 2022.

The average, however, hides what really matters: The curve began to rise again in September, concentrated in two state capitals, with a new strain of the virus circulating that is different from the one identified in the previous outbreak.
In virology, a clade is a group of viral lineages that share a common ancestor. Currently, clade Ib predominates among the samples analyzed. The 2022 mpox outbreak was caused by clade IIb.

In response, the Ministry of Health purchased 25,000 doses of the vaccine against the disease and instructed states and municipalities to administer it intradermally – that is, just into the top layer of skin. This technique can increase the number of people vaccinated with the same vial fivefold.
The vaccine has become even more important in the fight against mpox, because the only antiviral drug available to treat the disease has just failed two clinical trials.
What has changed about the virus?
Clade Ib was identified in 2023 in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and led the World Health Organization to declare an international public health emergency in August 2024.

Following a sustained decline in reported cases in Central and East Africa, the WHO declared the end of this international public health emergency. It was then that prevention, surveillance and control of the disease became part of long-term public health programs.

At the Fiocruz National Institute of Infectious Diseases, or INI/Fiocruz, a leading center for the disease in Rio, 43 of the 62 samples identified between September and October 2026 were from clade Ib. Of the total, only 19 were from clade IIb.

Clade Ib was first detected in Rio in March 2026. The spike in diagnoses did not occur until September. In October, the institute treated 130 people with suspected cases of the disease and confirmed 89 cases.
Clade Ib arrived in Brazil via travelers. INI/Fiocruz identified the first cases with evidence of community transmission – people infected locally, with no recent travel history – in early 2026.

The question is whether clade Ib would cause more severe illness. In Central Africa, it has been associated with a higher case fatality rate than that observed with clade IIb, but this difference is also linked to factors such as malnutrition, co-infections and lack of access to care.

In Rio, INI/Fiocruz has not yet found any clinically significant difference between the two clades in the group of patients being monitored, which they call the Rio cohort. The profile of the most vulnerable individuals remains the same – those with severe immunosuppression, pregnant women and young children. About 45% of the patients in the Rio cohort are living with HIV.
Antiviral drug failed the test

During the 2022 outbreak, the antiviral drug tecovirimat was distributed as a treatment for mpox. The drug had been approved in the U.S. for smallpox based on animal studies, since there was no way to test it on people, as smallpox had been eradicated from the planet since 1980. But the emergence of mpox has made it possible to approve the drug for people.

An April 2025 trial compared the drug tecovirimat with a placebo in 597 patients with clade I in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The time to lesions clearing up was seven days in the group that received tecovirimat and eight days in the placebo group. This difference is not considered statistically significant.

In February 2026, a second trial settled the question regarding clade II. The study followed more than 400 adults divided into two groups, one that received the antiviral and another that received a placebo. Through Day 29, the estimated rates of lesion resolution were similar in the two groups – 83% with tecovirimat and 84% with the placebo. The study found no evidence that tecovirimat was able to accelerate lesion resolution in adults with clade II mpox.

Thus, mpox remains a disease without a proven specific treatment, which shifts the focus of the response to early diagnosis, isolation and vaccination. The medication remains reserved for patients with severe cases and immunosuppressed patients, even though there is no evidence that it alters the course of the disease in these patients.

The only vaccine for mpox is MVA-BN, also known as Jynneos, a third-generation, nonreplicating smallpox vaccine produced by Bavarian Nordic in Denmark. It has not been tested in randomized trials to assess its efficacy against mpox. There are, however, observational studies conducted in the context of the 2022 outbreak, all involving clade IIb. In these studies, researchers do not determine who receives the vaccine, but simply monitor patient outcomes.

Based on these observational studies, the WHO estimates that this vaccine reduces the risk of mpox by 76% with one dose and by 82% with two, compared to unvaccinated individuals. Results varied from one study to another, particularly with a single dose. Estimates of risk reduction ranged from 35% to 86% with one dose and from 66% to 90% with two doses.
In the U.S., a cohort of at-risk transgender men and women estimated 89% protection with the full vaccination series and 70% with a single dose.

In another study in Germany, the effectiveness of a single dose was 58% overall, but only 35% among people living with HIV – a relevant finding for Brazil, given that nearly half of Brazilian cases occur in patients with HIV. This study also found that in those who have already been exposed, the vaccine reduces the risk of becoming ill by about 20% and appears to lessen the severity of the illness even when it does not prevent infection.

There are two weaknesses in these studies. The first concerns the duration of protection: Antibody levels drop sharply between six and 12 months after the second dose, although the cellular response persists. It is not yet known which of these indicators is a better predictor of protection.

The second is that there is no data on clinical efficacy against clade Ib, though there are laboratory studies. A British group showed in April 2026 that serum from 25 vaccinated healthcare workers neutralizes clade Ib, but at levels consistently lower than those observed against clade IIb. Cross-protection is likely, based on animal models challenged with clade I. The extent of this protection in humans, however, is unknown.

The intradermal injection method, now recommended by Brazil’s Ministry of Health, was adopted in the United States and Europe in 2022 – this method allows the use of one-fifth of the dose – and produced an immune response comparable to that of the subcutaneous method. The costs associated with the vaccine include personnel training and vials of the vaccine that, once thawed, must be used within four weeks.
Right now, prevention is the only way to contain mpox.

The purchase of vaccines for Brazil was made through the Pan American Health Organization Revolving Fund. The initial order of 20,000 doses was increased to 25,000 following negotiations with the manufacturer, with distribution scheduled to begin Nov. 23.

Prior to that, 3,650 doses from the national stockpile had already been shipped to nine states, including Rio de Janeiro, Ceará and the Federal District. The Unified Health System is limiting vaccination to specific groups: people living with HIV, users of preexposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, laboratory professionals who handle the virus, and medium- or high-risk contacts of confirmed cases. In line with WHO guidelines, there is no mass plan for vaccination. Vaccinations are administered at immunization reference centers rather than primary care clinics.

This decision is based on epidemiological logic and a practical constraint – the global shortage of the vaccine. But the bottleneck in Brazil has not always been supply. Between 2022 and 2023, the country distributed 49,000 doses of the mpox vaccine and administered 14,395 – less than a third.

In a survey of more than 9,500 people of different sexual orientations and gender identities, only 4.9% reported having received at least one dose. The researchers pointed to limited availability and barriers to access as likely explanations for the low coverage.

These same factors are likely to determine whether the 25,000 new doses will make a difference. To protect those at risk before exposure, the vaccine must reach these individuals in time for them to complete the two-dose regimen. This will require that the vaccine be available at facilities that offer PrEP for HIV and at the sexual health clinics these patients already attend – not just at public hospitals where they are unlikely to go.

In the meantime, the Ministry of Health is encouraging anyone who develops new skin lesions – especially if accompanied by a fever or swollen lymph nodes – to seek medical care and avoid close physical contact until they have been evaluated. They are also encouraging people with HIV to keep their antiretroviral therapy up to date, because immunosuppression, rather than the clade, determines who becomes severely ill with mpox.
This is a translation of this article from The Conversation Brazil. This version has been updated to reflect new case numbers at the time of publication.
Klinger Soares Faíco Filho is the founder of InfectoCast, a podcast dedicated to medical education.

articles.title: Doctors in Congress used to lean Republican – the 120th Congress marks a historic shift
articles.author: Michael E. Shepherd, Assistant Professor of Health Management and Policy, University of Michigan
paras: The 120th Congress, which will be sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027, will have 20 physicians as members, along with twice that number of members who have other professional health backgrounds.

This physician class will make history for including the most Democratic physicians in a single Congress – 11 – in American history – a marked shift from the Republican dominance of previous physician members. These Democratic physicians made their professional expertise and their health policy ideas centerpieces of their campaigns, and now they have the opportunity to advance their health policy agendas.

I am a political scientist who studies the partisan politics of health and health policy in the U.S. While physicians have long shaped American health policy, the physician class elected to the upcoming Congress is the most Democratic in the modern era.

The Democratic physician class in the Senate includes South Carolina’s Annie Andrews, a pediatrician. Andrews made reproductive health and rural healthcare access core tenets of her campaign. For instance, her campaign website stressed that “As a doctor and a mom, I’ve cared for women in some of the most difficult moments of their lives. … I’ll fight to: Restore the protections of Roe v. Wade, Guarantee access to contraception and infertility care, Expand maternal health services, especially in rural areas.”

In the House of Representatives, the Democratic physician class includes California’s Richard Pan, also a pediatrician. Pan’s campaign website, which featured many pictures and references to his physician background and stressed the importance of holding “RFK accountable for endangering Americans” – referring to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. – as well as fighting to lower prescription drug costs, preventing the continued withering of the Affordable Care Act and banning prior authorization.

Other Democratic medical doctors who will be serving in the 120th Congress include two newly elected members in the House, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey and Amish Shah of Arizona, in addition to six returning representatives. Newly elected to the Senate alongside Andrews is Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, an epidemiologist with a medical doctorate.

Beyond Congress, Democratic medical doctors will also serve as governors – with Amy Acton newly elected in Ohio and Josh Green reelected in Hawaii – as well as in numerous state legislative positions.
Doctors’ long history in politics

Physicians have played important roles in shaping American politics and health policies, back to the nation’s founding. For instance, Pennsylvania’s Dr. Benjamin Rush, an early public health advocate who led the city of Philadelphia through the yellow fever epidemic of 1793, was the only person with a medical degree to sign the Declaration of Independence.

Since the late 1980s, the number of physicians serving in Congress has increased substantially term over term. My colleagues and I have documented this rise, as well as how physician members of the House have influenced policy.

We found that physician members of the House were more active and effective in enacting health policy than other members. Physician members were more likely to sponsor health legislation, and their health bills advanced further in the legislative process. This was true for physicians from both parties, both on and off congressional health-related committees.

Since at least 1973, when our data begin, physician House members’ congressional voting behaviors and their health policies have been more conservative than other members on average, even those of their own parties. For example, we found that physician members were more likely to sponsor bills related to curbing abortion access, repealing the ACA and protecting private sector physician autonomy.

However, one of the most striking changes we observed was the shift from the Republican dominance of physician members of Congress to the steadily increasing number of Democratic physicians elected since 2015. That year, there were just two Democratic physicians in Congress, but the 119th Congress – 2025-2027 – has six Democratic physicians. The upcoming Congress will nearly double that amount, with the largest class of Democratic members with medical doctorates in American history.

It will be the first Democratic physician majority since 1995, during the 103rd Congress, when two out of the three physician House members were Democrats. Before 1995, physician members were much rarer, but the majority of them were Republicans. Between 1995 and 2023, 80% of physician members were Republicans.
These partisan changes reflect the broader partisan shifts within the medical community itself.
For most of the 20th century, the majority of physicians – both in Congress and more generally as a group – were Republicans. The American Medical Association was largely a conservative organization.
The party loyalties of today’s physician class mirror the slowly shifting demographics of physicians as a group.
Since the 1970s – and especially since the 1990s – medical school applicants and new physicians have become more diverse in terms of gender, race and ethnicity.

These groups tend to identify as Democrats at higher rates, though medicine as a field continues to be dominated by white men. Additionally, becoming a physician obviously requires getting an undergraduate and a professional degree, but higher educational attainment alone has also become increasingly related to Democratic support.
Beyond these more glacial demographic changes, three Trump-era events have shaped the political mobilization of Democratic physicians.

First, the partisan politics of COVID-19 and especially the politicization of the COVID-19 vaccine, has been associated with decreasing trust in medicine and science from Republican-aligned voters and an increase in physicians’ Democratic support.

Second, the elevation of Kennedy as HHS secretary, whose own vaccine skepticism has long run contrary to medical science and the advice of physicians, further pitted many physicians against the Republican Party.

Finally, the Supreme Court’s decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health, which overturned the Constitutional right to abortion, also appears to have politically mobilized many OB-GYNs and other women’s health professionals in response to threats to the care they provide and their professional livelihoods.
All these factors have contributed to a new physician class in Congress that is more Democratic and liberal in their health policy views than previous years.

Ultimately, what this difference means for future public policy remains to be seen. However, if politicians’ campaign priorities portend their legislative activity, there may be a more active push than Congress has ever seen for health reforms related to reproductive healthcare, rural health, prescription drug pricing, bans on prior authorization requirements by health insurers and maybe even Medicare for all.

articles.title: Cosmetic surgery is on the rise globally, with social media and celebrities reducing taboos and influencing beauty ideals
articles.author: Scott Hollenbeck, Professor of Plastic Surgery, University of Virginia
paras: Nearly 18 million cosmetic surgeries were performed worldwide in 2025, increasing by roughly 25% since 2021.

Without question, social media has had a significant impact on the global perception of plastic surgery. Surgeons and patients commonly share detailed stories about cosmetic surgery experiences, and celebrities around the world are increasingly candid about their own procedures. This openness has reduced the taboo surrounding this once hidden area of self-investment.

One of us is a medical student, and the other is a practicing plastic surgeon who previously served as president of the American Society of Plastic Surgeons. Through our research, we have identified a few key themes shaping cosmetic surgery globally.

Notably, social media has created some shared aesthetic trends, such as “Instagram Face.” Popularized by filters, this look is defined by full lips and high cheekbones, blending features from different ethnicities into one aesthetic.
But cultural identity continues to influence regional beauty standards, reflected in the different types of procedures prioritized around the world.
Facial procedures in South Korea
South Korea, often called the plastic surgery capital of the world, performs more cosmetic surgeries per capita than any other country, at roughly 16 procedures per 1,000 people.
It is also a major destination for medical tourism. About 1 in 10 cosmetic surgery patients in South Korea travel from abroad, primarily from China, Japan and the U.S.
In this market, K-pop and K-drama celebrities are widely seen as setting the standard for beauty.

More than 70% of cosmetic surgeries in South Korea are facial procedures. The most popular and well-known procedure is double eyelid surgery, which creates a crease in the upper eyelid, a feature that about half of East Asians are born without. Other common procedures include facial fat grafting, brow lifts and rhinoplasties.

Cosmetic surgery is widely accepted in South Korean culture, and it is viewed as an investment for social and professional success, rather than an act of vanity. One survey found that 90% of South Korean women ages 20 to 69 had been exposed to cosmetic surgery advertising.
China redefines engagement

China’s cosmetic surgery market is one of the fastest growing in the world, with 1.4 million cosmetic surgeries performed in 2025 – a rate of 1 surgery per 1,000 people. As in South Korea, procedures were predominantly focused on the face, and the No. 1 procedure was eyelid surgery.

A survey of Chinese female college students found that the top influences in getting cosmetic surgery were peers, pressure to stand out in an extremely competitive job market and social media exposure.

Social media has helped codify and perpetuate specific beauty ideals. For example, the term “melon seed face” was coined to describe the traditional Chinese beauty standard of an oval face shape with a slim, V-shaped jawline.

China’s plastic surgery market is simultaneously redefining how consumers find and access procedures. More than 60,000 plastic surgery clinics use platforms like Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, to advertise their services.
Dedicated cosmetic surgery apps such as GengMei and SoYoung increase accessibility by using AI to analyze users’ faces, connecting them with local clinics and even helping finance surgery payments.

While Brazil is the seventh-largest country in the world by population, it ranks first in the total number of cosmetic procedures performed globally. This market performed approximately 2.4 million surgeries at a rate of 11 per 1,000 people in 2025.

In contrast to South Korea and China, which emphasize facial procedures, Brazil’s market is defined by body contouring. In fact, this is true for much of Latin America. Liposuction – a surgery that uses suction to remove body fat – is the most commonly performed procedure, followed by breast augmentations and abdominal and buttock procedures.

Brazil’s emphasis on body shape and lower body aesthetics is so well known that it inspired the name of one of the world’s most popular procedures – the Brazilian Butt Lift, or BBL – despite the fact that it may not have actually originated in Brazil.

Cosmetic surgery in Brazil is highly accessible across all socioeconomic classes, rooted in the philosophy that everyone has a “right to beauty.” Brazil is one of the only countries where public hospitals offer cosmetic surgery for free to those who cannot afford it.

The U.S. ranked second globally in cosmetic surgery volume, just behind Brazil, with approximately 2.2 million procedures in 2025, at a rate of about 6.5 surgeries per 1,000 people. And like Brazil, the U.S. predominantly performs body contouring surgeries over facial surgeries.

The U.S. is unique in that it performs the highest number of nonsurgical procedures, such as fillers, botox and chemical peels. This may reflect a growing preference for subtle changes through minor, short-term treatments over major surgical makeovers.
Hair transplants in Turkey

Turkey is one of the world’s top destinations for medical tourism. According to Turkey’s Ministry of Health, more than 1.5 million people traveled to Turkey for medical procedures in 2024, generating US$3 billion in revenue.

This is largely driven by Turkey’s hair transplant industry, with numerous high-volume clinics offering low-cost procedures and travel packages. The Turkish Health Tourism Association estimated 1 million tourists spent $2 billion for hair transplants in 2022 alone.

Besides hair transplants, Turkey performs approximately 800,000 cosmetic surgeries annually, at a rate of nine surgeries per 1,000 people. Roughly 30% of patients travel from abroad for these procedures, primarily from Germany, the U.K. and the U.S.

Innovations in surgical techniques, technology and marketing have made cosmetic procedures more attainable to the average person. Cosmetic surgery is likely to continue growing as social media and cultural normalization help remove the mystery and secrecy surrounding these procedures.

articles.title: The DRC’s Ebola crisis revives an old ethical question: What do health workers owe patients?
articles.author: Baldeep K. Dhaliwal, Research Fellow in Global Infectious Disease Ethics, Johns Hopkins University
paras: The World Health Organization declared the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak on May 15, 2026. As of Nov. 18, there have been 11,712 cases and 5,720 deaths, nearly all in the Democratic Republic of Congo, or DRC.
Since the outbreak was declared, medical researchers have been racing to develop a vaccine that will work against this strain of Ebola, and trials are underway.

But in the absence of medical countermeasures, such as vaccines or therapeutic drugs, early detection and supportive care have been essential to reducing both the number of cases and the number of fatalities during this outbreak.

This care has required high levels of coordination and support among physicians, nurses, janitorial and environmental sanitation staff, public health practitioners, volunteers and community health workers, among others. These health workers have been asked to care for their communities at great personal cost. As of August 2026, 160 health workers had contracted Ebola, and 43 had died.
These deaths raise one of the oldest questions in bioethics: What do health workers owe patients during an outbreak?

We are an epidemiologist and a bioethicist, and we’ve been considering this question, alongside the question of how to keep workers safe during the current Ebola outbreak. We believe that worker protection is not an ethical add-on to outbreak control; it is a prerequisite for it.
A history of ethical codes and obligations

In 1847, the American Medical Association’s first code of ethics instructed physicians to keep working during outbreaks, “even at the risk of their own lives.” This rule was reiterated and strengthened in later versions of the code.

Up to that time, there had been a history of some physicians choosing to leave rather than support a widespread outbreak, ranging from the Antonine plague outbreak of 165-180 to the 1793 yellow fever epidemic in Philadelphia.

Ethical codes and guidelines give healthcare workers a shared set of principles that they can lean on, particularly when they have to make decisions in high-stress situations, to protect the community and to keep themselves safe.

Since the 1847 code, the debate over health workers’ duty to treat in the face of a contagious disease outbreak has turned on how much risk they can be asked to bear. Through outbreaks of HIV, SARS and COVID-19, that debate has resurfaced, with questions grounded in whether health workers have a moral obligation to act in the best interest of others; if they gave implied consent when they entered their professions; if the specialized training they have makes them uniquely qualified to provide care; and if the social contract they entered with the public, in exchange for reciprocal benefits such as priority access to vaccines, justifies their labor.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, some ethicists argued that the duty to care is real but conditional, depending on the availability of adequate protective equipment and on the state’s ability to respond to a pandemic and safeguard health workers.
Violence against health workers
But these conditions typically make two assumptions: first, that the main danger to a health worker is an infection, and second, that the health worker is a licensed clinician.

Recent research on violence against health workers has focused on physicians, trainees and nurses in emergency departments or psychiatric units, and more recent research highlights similar experiences throughout and following the COVID-19 pandemic.

But when an outbreak begins in places affected by prolonged, violent conflict, such as the eastern DRC, the primary danger to health workers is not necessarily the disease itself. Those responding to the Bundibugyo outbreak have also faced the anger of patients and affected communities, including physical and sexual assault and psychological violence, threats or intimidation. And that’s in addition to the downstream effects of protracted insecurity and armed and systemic violence, such as the criminalization of providing healthcare, abduction, arson, armed attacks and violent searches and theft.

The World Health Organization’s surveillance system for attacks on health care recorded 81 attacks since the declaration of the Bundibugyo outbreak in May 2026 through Nov. 18, 2026, resulting in five deaths and 34 injuries. These numbers include 29 attacks on facilities and warehouses, which have exacerbated already precarious resource shortfalls.

This data reflects only those attacks that have been reported to and verified by the surveillance system, so it does not necessarily give a complete picture of violent events. The reality as reported on the ground is even bleaker. As of August 2026, U.N. Senior Ebola Coordinator Julien Harneis reported that there had been over 260 attacks on health workers, and eight health workers had been killed.

Some clinics and health workers have been caught up in the political violence in the DRC, a complex conflict with roots in the lingering effects of Belgian colonization and the extractive industries that have exploited the area’s resources and left poverty and political instability in their wake. But some have been targeted due to community fear and mistrust. Many locals do not believe the care centers are safe, and they are upset that they cannot bury friends and family members who die from Ebola using normal burial rites and procedures, which may involve practices such as washing the body, which could spread the virus.
But what about the front-line health workers who aren’t licensed clinicians?

Most of the existing guidance in healthcare, such as the Hastings Center’s COVID-19 framework and the WHO’s guidance on ethical issues in outbreaks, is aimed at licensed clinicians working in clinical settings.

However, these organizations don’t provide ethical guidance to the community health workers, volunteers and cleaning staff who are often the most exposed in an outbreak. Many are paid through incentives rather than salaries, and they may travel alone to complete their work. Many are also women who face gendered harassment and assault on top of the risks their male colleagues share.

Though these workers occupy less formalized or protected positions within the health system, they are central to its efforts. But right now, the ethical frameworks that protect health workers – and the legal and societal obligations that follow from them – do not extend to these workers.

We believe there needs to be a balance: The safety of front-line workers cannot be sacrificed or overlooked in complex emergencies, and the urgent need to contain outbreaks cannot be valued more than the ethical duty to protect the health workers carrying out that response.
If health workers’ duty to treat depends on the state’s duty to protect, then protection from violence is the most basic protection to which a health worker is entitled.

In 1847, physicians were told to keep working, even when their own lives were at risk from the pathogen. But the risks confronting health workers in the Bundibugyo crisis today extend beyond infectious threats. Some are being asked to continue working even when they face the possibility of violence from armed actors, the community and the broader insecurities of protracted conflict.

When health workers – clinicians or not – are in unsafe conditions, disease surveillance and contact tracing stall, treatment capacity shrinks, communities lose access to trusted sources of care, and health workers face potentially higher risk of infection. In a conflict-affected crisis like the current Bundibugyo outbreak in the eastern DRC, protecting the workforce is part of containment.

articles.title: Flu and other winter viruses can hit older adults harder – here’s what you need to know
articles.author: Fran Ludwig, Associate Head, Biosciences and Chemistry,, Sheffield Hallam University
paras: “Put a coat on or you’ll catch a cold.” It is a familiar warning, but it leaves out the most important character in the story, the virus.

Colds are caused by viruses, so cold air alone cannot give you one. In winter, though, viruses can spread more easily indoors, and cold, dry air may make some of the body’s early defences less effective.

For older people, there is a further concern. Infections such as flu and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), a common virus that can cause a runny nose or a cough, are more likely to lead to serious illness in this age group.

In colder weather, people often spend more time together indoors with the windows shut. In rooms where little fresh air comes in, tiny particles carrying viruses can build up in the air, making it easier for an infection to pass from one person to another.
If you’re unwell with a respiratory infection, put off visiting anyone at higher risk until you feel better. When you do get together indoors, open a window for a few minutes to help clear the air.

Some of the body’s first defences are inside the nose and airways, the passages that carry air to the lungs. Mucus, the sticky fluid that coats these passages, traps particles, including viruses, and tiny, hair-like structures sweep the mucus along so the body can get rid of it. These hair-like structures act like a tiny conveyor belt, helping clear viruses before they can establish an infection. A 2024 review of research on indoor air found that dry conditions can slow this process.

If a virus does infect a cell, another defence comes into play. Infected cells can send out chemical signals that warn neighbouring cells and help them protect themselves. This can limit how far the virus spreads.

A 2024 study found that some cold viruses multiplied more easily in cells from the nose when they were kept at lower temperatures. The cells also produced a weaker early immune response to the virus. But the study was done in laboratory conditions, so it doesn’t tell us whether being out in the cold makes someone more likely to catch a cold.
Serious illness in older people

The immune system, which helps the body fight infections, changes with age. Some of its cells become less effective, and the body can make fewer of the protective proteins called antibodies that help stop a virus from infecting cells. At the same time, the body’s reaction to infection can become harder to regulate. If it goes on too long, it can damage the tissues it is trying to protect.

Long-term heart or lung conditions can make an infection harder to cope with. Cold air can also narrow the airways, making breathing harder, and cold weather can raise blood pressure, putting extra strain on the heart. Flu can lead to pneumonia or make an existing heart or lung condition worse.
Vaccines give the immune system a head start by helping it recognise a virus and respond more quickly. Vaccines against flu, COVID and RSV can reduce the risk of serious illness.

Because flu viruses change and protection fades, the NHS offers a flu vaccine every year to people aged 65 and over and others at higher risk. In England, eligibility for COVID vaccination and RSV vaccination depends on factors such as age and health.
Most colds get better on their own. If you are 65 or over and have flu symptoms, the NHS advises asking your GP surgery for an urgent appointment or contacting NHS 111.

If you are in a group at highest risk of serious illness from COVID and develop symptoms, take a rapid COVID test as soon as possible, even if the symptoms are mild. If the test is positive, contact your GP surgery, NHS 111 or your hospital specialist promptly. Medicines for COVID need to be started early.

When checking on an older relative or neighbour, pay attention to whether they seem like their usual self. Older people can have flu without a high temperature. In someone who is already frail, going off their food or behaving differently can be a sign of illness.

New confusion or unusual drowsiness can be signs of serious illness. If someone is more short of breath than usual, seek urgent advice from their GP surgery or NHS 111. If they become suddenly confused, are difficult to wake or are struggling to breathe, call 999 immediately.

articles.title: Norovirus is spreading – how to recognise the symptoms and what to do
articles.author: Charlotte Lewis, PhD Candidate, Virology, University of Glasgow
paras: Described as the “Ferrari of the virus world” for the way it races from person to person, norovirus is once again on the move as we head into winter.

Reports from the UK Health Security Agency have highlighted that cases of norovirus – commonly known as the “winter vomiting bug” – have increased by more than 35% in England over the past two weeks, compared with the previous fortnight.

While that sounds alarming, this is still within expected levels for the season. Overall case numbers are about 5% above what’s typical for this time of year. Cases have fallen in Scotland, but Wales has seen a rise.
Norovirus symptoms include sudden-onset nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting, sometimes accompanied by fever, stomach pain, body aches and headaches.

Most healthy adults recover within one to three days. However, those with weakened immune systems, older adults and young children face a higher risk of severe symptoms. When this happens, people can be ill for much longer and may need hospital treatment if they become dehydrated.

Norovirus is highly contagious, with some studies suggesting that as few as ten virus particles can cause an infection. It spreads from person to person when tiny amounts of virus from infected faeces or vomit get on to food, hands or surfaces and are then transferred to the mouth.

Close contact between people can also spread the virus. This may help explain why cases peak in winter, when people spend more time together indoors. However, you can catch it at any time of the year.
The virus is also particularly resilient; it can survive on hard kitchen surfaces such as stainless steel and ceramic for up to two weeks, and it takes temperatures of around 60°C to kill it.

There are no approved vaccines or specific treatments for norovirus. It evolves quickly to escape our immune systems, and has proved notoriously difficult to grow in the lab, which has hampered research efforts. That said, recent breakthroughs in growing norovirus using lab-grown human gut cells may make it easier to develop treatments in future.
How to protect yourself and your household

While alcohol-based hand sanitisers can be effective against other viruses, such as the ones that cause COVID and flu, they don’t work well against norovirus. Instead, the best way to protect yourself is by washing your hands often with soap and hot water, ideally for 15 seconds or more. This is particularly important before or after preparing food, and after going to the toilet.

Norovirus is also frequently spread through contaminated food. Fresh produce such as fruit and vegetables may pick up the virus during harvesting, packaging or handling, so wash these thoroughly before use. Shellfish such as oysters can also be contaminated with concentrated norovirus from the water they live in, so ensure these are thoroughly cooked, rather than steamed or eaten raw.
If someone in your household has norovirus, cleaning surfaces regularly with bleach-based products can help prevent the virus from spreading.

Using a dummy called Vomiting Larry, researchers found that norovirus-containing droplets can spread around ten feet (three metres) when someone vomits. So, it’s important to immediately clean areas that have been contaminated by vomit or faeces.

Frequent cleaning of heavily used surfaces such as door handles, light switches, taps, toilet seats and flush handles, ideally while wearing disposable gloves, can help reduce the chances of the virus spreading.
Washing soiled clothes or bedding separately from other laundry, at a temperature of 60°C or above at the longest cycle time possible, can also help kill the virus on soft surfaces.
If you are unlucky enough to get norovirus yourself, the only solution is to allow the virus to run its short, but deeply unpleasant, course.

Replacing lost fluids is essential, so drink plenty of water, tea or electrolyte drinks, or use oral rehydration sachets. If you feel able to eat, stick to plain foods that are easy to digest, such as toast, rice, pasta or soup, and avoid fatty or salty foods that may make your symptoms worse.

As norovirus is highly contagious, ensure that you stay at home and rest as much as possible. Keep your distance from other people in your household where you can, and avoid preparing food for others while you’re unwell and for at least 48 hours after symptoms stop.
Even after full recovery, infectious virus can still be shed in poo for up to two weeks, so continuing to frequently clean bathroom areas can help prevent further transmission.
With cases rising as winter sets in, the Ferrari of viruses may be doing the rounds for a while yet. A few simple habits could save you, and others, a very unpleasant few days.

articles.title: Pimple-popping videos can be disgusting – and strangely satisfying
articles.author: Katie Edwards, Commissioning Editor, Health + Medicine and Host of Strange Health podcast, The Conversation
paras: Some people relax by watching someone squeeze pus from a stranger’s face. I’m one of them. I have favourite accounts, strong opinions about technique and very little patience for a video that ends before the pore has been properly cleared.

I tend to watch with the sound off and the speed doubled, slowing things down if a particularly promising spot needs closer attention. My hairdresser discovered this interest when she caught sight of my phone. She was considerably less enthusiastic.
But why does something that makes one person recoil keep another watching? And are people like me less easily disgusted in the first place?

In the latest episode of Strange Health, The Conversation’s podcast about unusual health and wellness trends, I explore pimple popping with my co-host Dan Baumgardt, a practising GP and lecturer at the University of Bristol.

Our guest is Albert Wabnegger, a scientist at the University of Graz in Austria who specialises in the psychology of disgust. He doesn’t particularly enjoy pimple-popping videos himself, but has spent rather more time studying them than most non-fans would volunteer for.
Measuring the pleasure of a popped pimple

Wabnegger and his colleagues developed a questionnaire to measure how much people enjoy popping their own spots or watching someone else’s being squeezed. He takes me through it during the episode. I rapidly develop concerns that the scale doesn’t go high enough.

For a study involving 80 women, the researchers showed enthusiasts and non-enthusiasts pimple-popping videos inside a brain scanner. For comparison, they showed water spraying from fountains and steam cleaners removing dirt from cars and stone floors.

Fans of pimple-popping videos reported more pleasure and less disgust while watching, although they still felt some disgust. On a separate questionnaire, the two groups gave similar ratings when asked how disgusting they found situations that might expose them to germs. Fans did report fewer difficulties managing feelings of disgust. The scans also revealed differences in activity in a brain region involved in motivation and reward.
Wabnegger explains why that needs careful interpretation. Brain activity cannot tell researchers precisely what somebody feels, and these findings don’t demonstrate a dopamine rush.
Enjoying disgust from a safe distance
One possible explanation involves the safety of the screen. Watching a pimple being squeezed puts you close enough to see everything without any chance of its contents reaching you.
Wabnegger compares this with enjoying a horror film: an uncomfortable experience can become entertaining when the viewer feels safe.

His later research has also linked pimple-popping enjoyment with morbid curiosity, an interest in disturbing or threatening subjects. That association offers a possible clue to the appeal, rather than establishing why any individual watches.
Some viewers say the videos help them relax. Wabnegger wants to investigate what prompts people to seek them out and how they feel afterwards. Whether watching helps people sleep remains untested.
Listen to the episode for the science behind this divisive viewing habit, and my increasingly unsubtle attempts to secure a place in his next experiment.

articles.title: Brain lesions: what causes them and when they need follow-up
articles.author: Gavin Giovannoni, Professor of Neurology, Centre for Neuroscience, Surgery and Trauma, Queen Mary University of London
paras: You open your brain scan report and see the word “lesion”. It’s a worrying word to come across while waiting to speak to your doctor.

In a report, it means there’s an area in or around the brain that looks abnormal on the scan. That could be anything from an area of tissue damaged by a stroke to a pocket of fluid that’s been there for years.
What happens next depends on what the radiologist thinks they’re looking at.

Take a stroke. If a clot blocks an artery supplying the brain, the tissue downstream is starved of oxygen. Brain cells can die, leaving an area of damage that doctors call an infarct. Even a tiny stroke in an area that controls movement can leave someone with lasting weakness. If your face suddenly droops on one side or you develop arm weakness or trouble speaking, call 999 straight away, even if the symptoms pass.

A lesion can also form through inflammation. In multiple sclerosis (MS), the immune system attacks myelin, the protective coating around nerve fibres. Damage to that coating makes it harder for messages to travel along the nerves. The damaged areas can show up on MRI scans in the brain or spinal cord. Doctors look at where those areas are and what pattern they form, because several other conditions can produce spots on an MRI.

Sometimes the lesion is a growth. A meningioma is a tumour that starts in the protective layers of tissue around the brain. Most meningiomas are non-cancerous and grow slowly. They can go unnoticed for years and turn up on a scan that’s being carried out for another reason. Even a non-cancerous tumour can cause symptoms if it presses on the brain.
What the scan can tell you about a lesion

If you’ve ever looked at a set of MRI images, you might have noticed that the fluid around the brain can look bright in one picture and dark in another. Think of how an Instagram filter makes some details stand out. The MRI scanner does something similar by changing how it captures the image.

Radiologists call these different settings “sequences”. One can turn down the signal from the fluid so that patches of abnormal tissue next to it stand out. Another is sensitive to the movement of water within tissue and can help pick up a recent stroke.

Sometimes the radiologist will go looking for an older scan. If the same area looked exactly the same several years ago, that gives them information a single scan can’t. If there’s no earlier scan to compare it with, a repeat scan may help show whether the lesion is changing over time.
When a brain lesion needs follow-up

Some findings on a scan can be left alone. An arachnoid cyst is a pocket of fluid in one of the membranes around the brain. On a scan, it typically has a clear outline, and the fluid inside looks the same as the fluid that normally surrounds the brain. In adults, a small cyst with these features often needs no further scans if it causes no symptoms and is in a place where it’s unlikely to block the flow of fluid.

For some lesions, a repeat scan helps doctors see whether they’re growing. If a meningioma is found by chance and is causing no symptoms, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence suggests a repeat scan after a year. If the tumour looks the same, clinicians can consider ending follow-up or scanning again five years after it was first found.
If the scan shows a brain abscess, a pocket of pus in the brain caused by an infection, the next step is urgent treatment in hospital.

If you’re reading your own report, look for the summary, often headed “impression” or “conclusion”. That’s where the radiologist usually gives their best explanation of what they’ve seen and may suggest a next step. When you speak to the clinician who arranged the scan, ask what they think caused the lesion and whether you need to do anything about it. If they recommend another scan, ask what they’ll be looking for.

articles.title: From novels to GTA 6: the long history of fears about addictive entertainment
articles.author: James O'Sullivan, Professor of Digital Culture & Cultural Analytics, University College Cork
paras: The release of Grand Theft Auto VI, arguably the most anticipated video game in history, has prompted warnings about excessive gaming. Addiction specialists have urged players to recognise when gaming begins to interfere with their lives, while experts have raised concerns about its potential effects on younger players. These warnings reflect broader concerns about gaming addiction, rather than evidence that GTA VI itself is particularly addictive.

There are genuine health concerns behind these fears. The World Health Organization recognises gaming disorder as a condition wherein someone loses control over their gaming, prioritising it to the extent that there are serious consequences.

Taking a sneaky sick day for a marathon gaming session when a new game launches isn’t the issue. Gaming disorder is far more serious. It involves significant disruption to someone’s personal life, relationships, education or work.

Gaming disorder is a recognised health condition, and researchers have investigated how common it is. But the broader fear that people might become so absorbed in fictional worlds that they neglect everyday life predates video games. Similar concerns were once directed at other forms of entertainment, including novels.

As novels became increasingly popular during the eighteenth century, they attracted the same criticism that video games receive today. In Germany, commentators coined the term “Lesesucht”, meaning “reading addiction” or “reading mania”, to describe what they saw as an unhealthy obsession with books.

In England, critics worried that people would spend too much time reading novels and struggle to distinguish fiction from reality. Young women were considered particularly vulnerable, with fears that romantic stories might corrupt their morals or encourage unrealistic expectations about what they might expect from life.

Prominent writers joined the debate. In his autobiography Biographia Literaria, the poet and critic Samuel Taylor Coleridge criticised readers of popular fiction for losing themselves in daydreams rather than thinking critically about what they read. Jane Austen, meanwhile, defended novels as a serious form of literature in Northanger Abbey.

The fears continued as new forms of entertainment emerged. During the 19th century, cheap adventure and crime stories known as penny dreadfuls in Britain and dime novels in America were blamed for encouraging juvenile crime.

In 1954, following growing concerns about the influence of horror and crime comics on children, the American comics industry established the Comics Code Authority, which imposed restrictions on what publishers could show.

Later, critics accused television of turning audiences into passive viewers and taking time away from more worthwhile activities, including reading. More recently, streaming services and binge-watching have revived concerns about spending too much time absorbed in entertainment.
Although the form of entertainment changes, the underlying fear remains familiar: that popular stories can have a harmful influence on the people who enjoy them.

Novels and video games share an important attraction. Both can transport us into fictional worlds, allowing us to escape everyday life, explore unfamiliar experiences and become emotionally involved in stories.

Many historical fears about popular entertainment reflected the social attitudes and prejudices of their time. But fiction can influence how people see themselves and the world around them. It can shape expectations, encourage dissatisfaction with everyday life or offer an escape from problems that people would rather avoid.

Video games can be particularly absorbing because they allow players to take an active part in fictional worlds. Instead of simply following a story, players can explore, make decisions and influence what happens.

Some games also encourage people to keep playing by regularly introducing new challenges, rewards and items to collect. In Grand Theft Auto Online, the online version of GTA V, new vehicles and weapons were continually released, giving players reasons to return and avoid missing out.

This approach can also encourage spending. Players can use real money to purchase in-game currency, which can then be spent on virtual items. Such features have helped make the franchise enormously profitable, with GTA V and its online component reportedly generating an estimated US$10 billion in revenue since the game’s release in 2013.

These commercial strategies raise important questions about how games are designed to keep people playing and spending money. For those already struggling to control their gaming, systems that offer frequent rewards and encourage repeated play may be particularly concerning.

However, gaming disorder affects a relatively small minority of people. A review of research from 17 countries estimated that around 2% of the general population experiences gaming disorder, although estimates varied considerably between studies.

Spending a lot of time playing video games does not, by itself, mean someone has an addiction. What matters is whether they have lost control over their gaming and whether it is causing serious problems in their everyday life.

Gaming can provide an escape from difficult circumstances, just as books, television and other forms of entertainment can. The reasons someone plays, and the effects gaming has on their life, are therefore more revealing than the number of hours they spend doing it.

So, if you or someone you know is currently spending a lot of time in Vice City, you probably needn’t worry. We shouldn’t judge someone’s gaming habits simply by counting the hours they play, any more than we would judge their reading habits by counting the pages they finish.

Someone pretending to have a cold to get a day off work for a new game’s release may simply be enjoying a rare occasion. But if they repeatedly miss work, neglect relationships or struggle to stop playing despite serious consequences, there may be cause for concern.
